plan.day: Teaching a class all morning, then parent video calls on my phone in the afternoon

moments.title: Teaching the class
assumptions: I took the classroom as indoor light with the class at the default presenting distance.

notice.text: At 4 m in indoor light, about 1 in 10 dark spots and about 1 in 8 fine lines could be picked out by a typical viewer.
Redness, under-eye shadows and under-eye puffiness are noticeable at 4 m, and no free change hides them.

outOfSight.text: Breakouts and pores are out of sight for a typical viewer at 4 m in indoor light.

claim.text: No free change helps here, and no measured makeup plan exists for redness, so nothing is suggested for this moment.

moments.title: Parent video calls
assumptions: I assumed the phone is held at arm's length and you appear alone in speaker view.

notice.text: At 1.6 m in video call light, most dark spots and about a third of breakouts could be picked out by a typical viewer.
Redness, under-eye shadows and under-eye puffiness are noticeable on the call.

outOfSight.text: The video cannot carry detail finer than 0.72 mm, so 190 of 207 fine lines are below what the camera shows.
143 of 221 pores are also below what the camera can carry.

claim.text: No free change works; for dark spots, 100% coverage measured in indoor light at 1.5 m gives most of the effect, not all of it.

summary.text: Across your day, breakouts and pores stay out of sight while teaching at 4 m, and the phone video cannot carry 190 of 207 fine lines.

assumptions: Distance: Presenting to a room. Hall (1966): public distance begins at 3.7 m. The model's profiles end at 6 m.
Light: indoor light. An office or a well-lit room, roughly 400 lux on the face. Project assumption: skin is a matte surface that reflects about 35% of the light that falls on it.
Viewer: a typical person with 20/20 sight, looking right at the mark, with nothing else competing for their attention.
'About' numbers are for an average observer. 'At most' numbers are for even perfect eyes (a 6 dB margin on top of the average observer), so a real viewer sees the same or less.
Sizes in millimetres use your iris as the ruler (about 4% uncertainty), so they carry that uncertainty too.
Masks and contrasts come from one photo; hair, glasses, make-up, movement and a different angle will change what is seen.

quotes.change: no free change is enough to reach that here
quotes.limit: even 6 m apart in evening light at home, redness (noticeable) would still be picked out

Light: video call light. On a video call the other person's eyes are adapted to a screen of 200 to 300 cd/m2, and a face on it is about 0.35 of white.

Project assumption: a phone's front camera is roughly 80 degrees diagonal; held upright with a 3:4 frame that is about 67 degrees along the long, vertical side.

Selfies are typically taken at about 30 cm (Ward et al. 2018, JAMA Facial Plast Surg 20(4)); about 35 cm is taken for a call (Project assumption). The most is an arm's length, about 70 cm (Project assumption).
Project assumption: they sit about 60 cm from a laptop screen, inside the 50 to 100 cm usually advised for monitor distance (OSHA computer workstations guidance).
Project assumption: on a 15-inch laptop screen (about 19 cm tall) a speaker view fills about 17 cm and a gallery tile of four to nine people about 7 cm.

Project assumption: an upright phone sends 720 by 1280 to a large tile and 360 by 640 to a small gallery tile, so the long side is the vertical. The smallest detail the video carries is taken as two rows of pixels.
The whole camera frame is assumed to fill the height of the tile.
Video compression hides more than this removes, so the distance is a cautious estimate: the real picture is, if anything, softer.
Marks smaller than the video's smallest detail are counted as lost in the video, whatever the other person's eyes.

quotes.measuredAt: measured in indoor light at 1.5 m
quotes.goal: at most 1 in 10 picked out by perfect eyes
quotes.result: most of the effect, not all of it

assumptions: Measured in indoor light, at 1.5 m, with a typical viewer looking right at it.
This is a virtual try-on of foundation, run once on your photo; real makeup, shade and light will differ.
Coverage is the try-on's own scale from 0 to 100, not a property of any product on a shelf.
The goal is that even perfect eyes could pick out at most 1 in 10 of them across a table; where makeup cannot reach that, the coverage shown is where most of the effect is reached.
